destination.title: She memorized her attacker's face to be certain

short30: In a courtroom she looked at the man who attacked her and swore she was certain.
In 1984, in Burlington, North Carolina, a college student named Jennifer Thompson was attacked at knifepoint.
She forced herself to memorize her attacker's face.
Police showed her a photo lineup, then a live lineup, and both times she chose a man named Ronald Cotton.
But Cotton was the only person who appeared in both lineups.
By the live lineup, she may have been recognizing the police photo, not her attacker.
Detectives told her she'd done great — and that quiet reassurance hardened a careful guess into total certainty.
In 1985, it sent Cotton to prison.
He served more than a decade.
Then in 1995, DNA testing excluded Ronald Cotton and matched the real attacker — a lookalike inmate named Bobby Poole, who later pleaded guilty.
Here is the part no one expects: he and Jennifer became close friends and advocates who helped reform how police run a lineup.
Watch the full story on the channel.

candidate_payload_lines: She had never been more certain of anything in her life.
In the summer of 1984, in Burlington, North Carolina, a twenty-two-year-old college student named Jennifer Thompson was attacked in her own apartment at knifepoint.
In the middle of the worst night of her life, she made a decision that most people never could.
None of this was a trick played on a foolish woman.
In 1985, it was enough to convict Ronald Cotton and to send him to prison for the rest of his life.
But inside the prison, something happened that stories like this almost never give you.
It would take a science that, in 1984, had barely been born.
The physical evidence from the case had been preserved, and in 1995 it was finally sent for testing to a lab in Burlington called **LabCorp**.
On June 30th, 1995, after more than a decade behind bars for a crime he did not commit, Ronald Cotton walked out of prison.
And in 1997, in a small church office, Jennifer Thompson finally sat down across from the man she had sent to prison.
She told him that even if she spent every remaining day of her life apologizing, it would never be enough.
The problem was never that Jennifer Thompson wasn't certain enough.
Jennifer Thompson has spent years now saying it out loud, so that no one can miss it: memory can be honest, and confident, and still be completely wrong.

The real perpetrator stood only a few feet away, and her memory did not so much as flicker.

Bobby Poole later pleaded guilty to the attacks.

lines.text: The meeting did not happen quickly. Ronald Cotton wanted to see her, and then he waited nearly two years, until she was ready.

But he waited — nearly two years — until she was ready.

lines.text: There is a room, somewhere, where the person who was wrong and the person who paid for it finally sit down together.

lines.text: A liar can be caught. But an honest witness who is certain and wrong carries no tell at all. In court, certainty wins.

lines.text: So ask how an honest witness ends up wrong. The answer starts with the one thing she did to make sure she never would.
